Oval, greenish-grey, wet-looking spots on the sheaths that grow and spread up the stem, with plants dying in round patches, are typical of it. Stem borer is unlikely because the central shoots are not dried. What you can do now: avoid adding more nitrogen, and ask your extension officer whether a fungicide is needed and which product and dose to use. Fungicides work best at the first signs of infection, and the same chemical shouldn't be used again and again. For next season, plant less densely, remove crop residues and infected stubble after harvest, and rotate with a non-rice crop.

seed_idea: Whiteheads at grain filling that slide out easily when pulled; no neck/node lesions, no leaf spots.
differential_reasoning: Stem borer - likely: whiteheads slide out easily; Rice blast - unlikely: blast whiteheads stay firm, and no neck or leaf lesions.

input.user_text: At grain filling, I have white, empty heads. When I pull them, the head and stem slide right out. There are no marks on the necks and no spots on the leaves.

target_response.user_response: This points to stem borer. White, empty heads that slide out easily when pulled are typical of stem-borer damage; blast whiteheads usually stay firmly attached, and blast would normally also leave greyish-brown lesions below the panicle or spots on the leaves. For next season: cut the crop at ground level at harvest and remove the stubble and volunteer rice so larvae don't carry over, choose your planting date carefully, use a resistant variety, and protect natural enemies such as small wasps. Pheromone traps that attract the males can also reduce numbers; your extension officer can advise.

seed_idea: 'The middle leaf of my plants is dead.' Ask for pull and squeeze tests.
differential_reasoning: Stem borer - possible: larvae bore into growing points, central leaf dies; Bacterial blight - possible: easily confused with stem-borer damage.

input.user_text: The middle leaf of a lot of my plants is dead. Why?

target_response.user_response: A dead middle leaf is often caused by stem borers feeding inside the shoot, but bacterial blight can look similar. Please check: (1) Gently pull a dead middle leaf: does it come out easily from the base? (2) Cut a wilted leaf and squeeze it: does a yellowish ooze come out? (3) Are there tiny holes in the stem, or larvae inside when you split one open? (4) How old is the crop? Then I can tell you what it is and what to do.

seed_idea: 'There are worms inside my rice stems.' Ask about deadhearts / whiteheads; splitting a stem for larvae is a recognised check.
differential_reasoning: Stem borer - likely: larvae inside the stem; damage level unknown (deadhearts / whiteheads?).

input.user_text: I opened some rice stems, and there are small worms inside. What are they, and are they a problem?

target_response.user_response: Small larvae inside rice stems are most likely stem borers; splitting stems to look for them is exactly how they are checked. To see how much damage they are doing: (1) Are there plants whose central shoot has dried up (deadhearts)? (2) Are there white, empty heads (whiteheads)? (3) How old is the crop? With that, I can suggest what to do.

seed_idea: 'Is it stem borer?' with only 'dead tillers' as evidence. Must not confirm without checks.
differential_reasoning: Stem borer - possible; Bacterial blight - possible (look-alike); Sheath blight - possible (kills tillers). Must not confirm without checks.

input.user_text: Some tillers in my field are dead. Is it the stem borer?

target_response.user_response: It could be, but dead tillers can also come from bacterial blight or sheath blight, so let's check before deciding. (1) Do the dead tillers pull out easily from the base? Stem-borer damage usually does; bacterial blight doesn't. (2) Cut and squeeze a wilted leaf: is there a yellowish ooze? (3) Are there greenish-grey spots on the sheaths? (4) Are there tiny holes in the stems? Tell me what you find.

seed_idea: Tillering crop: central shoots dried and brown, outer leaves green. Stem borer vs bacterial blight; ask pull + squeeze tests and whether the field is deepwater.
differential_reasoning: Stem borer - possible: drying of the central tiller (deadheart) at the vegetative stage; Bacterial blight - possible: causes wilting and drying and is easily confused with stem-borer damage

input.user_text: My rice is at the tillering stage. In many plants, the central shoot has dried up and turned brown, while the outer leaves are still green. What is causing this?

target_response.user_response: A dried central shoot is a typical sign of stem-borer damage (a 'deadheart'), but bacterial blight can also make plants wilt and dry, and the two are easily confused. Three quick checks will help: (1) Gently pull the dried central shoot. If it comes out easily from the base, that points to stem borer; shoots affected by bacterial blight are not easily pulled out. (2) Cut a wilted leaf and squeeze it: a yellowish ooze from the cut end points to bacterial blight. (3) Look for tiny holes in the stem, or split a damaged stem open to look for larvae and their droppings. Let me know what you find.

seed_idea: Broken, dried stems: stem borer vs node blast. Ask about banded node lesions.
differential_reasoning: Stem borer - possible: larvae penetrate nodes at booting, whorl turns brown and dry; Rice blast - possible: infected nodes break the culm.

input.user_text: Some stems in my field are broken and dried. The rice is at booting. What's doing this?

target_response.user_response: At booting, broken and dried stems can be caused by stem borers or by blast on the stem joints. Please check: (1) Is there a brown, grey or black band around the joint where the stem broke? That points to blast. (2) Are there tiny holes in the stem, or larvae inside when you split one open? That points to stem borer. (3) Does a dried shoot pull out easily from the base? Let me know what you see.

seed_idea: Dead central tillers; squeezed leaves give no ooze and sheaths have no lesions: bacterial blight and sheath blight less likely.
differential_reasoning: Stem borer - likely: deadheart; Bacterial blight - unlikely: no ooze; Sheath blight - unlikely: clean sheaths.

input.user_text: Many plants have a dead central tiller. I squeezed the leaves, and no ooze came out, and the sheaths look clean, with no spots.

target_response.user_response: This points to stem borer. A dead central tiller (deadheart) is typical of stem-borer feeding, and you have ruled out the two main lookalikes: there is no ooze, so bacterial blight is unlikely, and the sheaths are clean, so sheath blight is unlikely. If you want to be sure, a stem-borer deadheart usually pulls out easily from the base. What you can do now: raise the water level from time to time to drown eggs laid low on the plants, keep weeds down in and around the field, protect natural enemies such as small wasps, ants and lady beetles, and apply nitrogen in split doses. If you consider an insecticide, ask your extension officer which product and dose to use, and use it carefully, because it also kills the insects that eat stem borers. After harvest, remove the stubble and volunteer rice.

seed_idea: Farmer asks which insecticide to use and how much.
differential_reasoning: Stem borer - reported by the farmer, not yet checked; product and dose request.
escalation_reason: Product + dose request (no reviewed fact gives products or doses).

input.user_text: Stem borers are all over my rice. Which insecticide is best, and how many ml per litre?

target_response.user_response: I can't recommend a product or a dose, so please ask your local extension officer or plant protection office. Pesticides should be used carefully: overuse leads to resistance and harms the environment and people's health, and it also kills the natural enemies of stem borers. It's also worth confirming it really is stem borer: dead central shoots should pull out easily from the base, and you may find larvae if you split a damaged stem. Meanwhile, there are things you can do without chemicals: raise the water level from time to time to drown eggs low on the plants, protect natural enemies such as small wasps, and use pheromone traps to reduce numbers.

differential_reasoning: Stem borer - likely: deadhearts pull out easily, larva inside the stem; Bacterial blight - unlikely: no ooze.

What you can do now: raise the water level from time to time to drown eggs laid low on the plants, keep weeds down in and around the field, protect natural enemies such as small wasps, ants and lady beetles, and apply nitrogen in split doses.
